tier_reason: Independent third-party suite with public code (run-benchmarks.php builds and runs c/benchmark.c, cpp/benchmark.cpp and rust/src/main.rs, 10 runs averaged), compilers and versions in the README (gcc/g++ 7.5.0, rustc 1.51.0, regex 1.4.5, PCRE2 10.36-2, Boost 1.65.1), flags in run-benchmarks.php (gcc -O3 -DNDEBUG, g++ -std=c++11 -O3, cargo build --release) and the CPU identified (2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, MacBook Pro 16-inch 2019); upgraded from B to A on that basis.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'Performance' table (submitted code): Rust total 57.63 ms (email 26.66, URI 25.70, IP 5.28) vs C PCRE2 251.37 ms (126.10, 112.17, 13.10), C++ Boost 104.23 ms and C++ STL 1023.49 ms, i.e. 4.36x vs PCRE2 without JIT, 1.81x vs Boost.Regex and 17.76x vs std::regex (derived from page data). 'Optimized' branch table: Rust 27.94 ms (11.43, 11.40, 5.11) vs C PCRE2 with JIT 87.87 ms (46.22, 36.92, 4.73), C++ Boost 104.28 ms, C++ STL 1021.10 ms, i.e. 3.14x, 3.73x and 36.55x (derived from page data); PCRE2 JIT is faster than Rust on the IP pattern (4.73 vs 5.11 ms).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From run-benchmarks.php in Docker image mariomka/regex-benchmark:1.6 (Ubuntu 18.04): C PCRE2 'gcc -O3 -DNDEBUG c/benchmark.c -lpcre2-8' (gcc 7.5.0, prebuilt libpcre2-dev 10.36-2 package from the ondrej/php PPA); C++ 'g++ -std=c++11 -O3 cpp/benchmark.cpp' (g++ 7.5.0; Boost 1.65.1 regex from the Ubuntu libboost-regex-dev package, std::regex header-only from libstdc++); Rust 'cargo build --release' (rustc 1.51.0, regex 1.4.5, default opt-level 3). Build flags of the prebuilt PCRE2 and Boost.Regex libraries are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Library-versus-library comparison, not a language-level one: the regex crate is a finite-automaton engine while PCRE2, Boost.Regex and std::regex backtrack. The 'Original' C PCRE2 row runs without JIT: c/benchmark.c calls pcre2_compile and pcre2_match only, and commit 'Remove JIT from C & PCRE2 for following the default settings rule' (2020-05-03) removed it; the optimized branch adds pcre2_jit_compile/pcre2_jit_match and cuts PCRE2 to 87.87 ms, and there PCRE2 JIT beats Rust on the IP pattern. The optimized Rust code also sets unicode(false), which makes \w ASCII like PCRE2's default. Timing includes pattern compilation; one input text (Learn X in Y minutes docs) that the README says 'isn't the best representative text'; the runner averages 10 runs and does not cross-check match counts between languages. Toolchains are from 2021 (results committed 2021-04-01, rustc 1.51, gcc 7.5, PCRE2 10.36), run under Docker on macOS, and the benchmark repo is archived (last commit 2021-10-18, archived 2026-01-28); SRELL was added to the code in October 2021 without new results. PCRE2 and Boost.Regex are prebuilt distro packages, so their optimisation flags are unknown, while the harnesses are -O3 on every side. rust-lang/regex is already listed (wave 14, string-and-text, tier A) and nim-regex from the same table is catalogued (wave 3).
corrections.why_faster: Different engine design, not language codegen: Rust regex 1.4.5 matches with finite automata (lazy DFA, no backtracking) and is compiled from source at opt-level 3, while the C PCRE2 row runs PCRE2's backtracking interpreter without JIT under the suite's default-settings rule and Boost.Regex and std::regex are backtracking engines. Against PCRE2 with JIT (optimized branch) the gap narrows to 3.14x and reverses on the IP pattern.

notes: All numbers match the README tables; the record's 'compiler flags are not stated' is wrong because run-benchmarks.php gives them, hence the upgrade to A. Main shortcomings: the PCRE2 'Original' row is the non-JIT interpreter by the suite's rule, toolchains are from 2021, the comparison is engine against engine rather than language against language, and rust-lang/regex is already listed in wave 14 (the orchestrator may treat this row as a second claim on that entry).

tier_reason: Independent measurement: the Guigó lab's public Nextflow pipeline guigolab/sambamBench-nf (templates/<tool>/<version> command scripts, nextflow.config) ran sambamba 0.6.6 and 0.6.8-pre1 against samtools 1.3 and 1.7 in grape Singularity containers, and its 16-CPU/120 GB report (gh-pages report_16_120G.html) carries per-task wall times; CPU model and compiler flags are not stated, so not A. Tier stays B, but the README's headline claims are overstated (see corrections).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (quoting the CRG comparison): flagstat 1.4x faster than samtools, index similar, markdup almost 6x, view 4x, sort beaten by samtools but up to 2x faster on 120GB+ machines. The README's linked report (public-docs.crg.es sambamba_ws_report.html) could not be opened. The pipeline's own 16 CPU / 120 GB report gives wall times (realtime) vs samtools 1.7: flagstat 7.7 s (sambamba 0.6.8-pre1) and 11.4 s (0.6.6) vs 11.5 s, 1.49x and 1.00x; index 12.7 s and 14.9 s vs 13.1 s, 1.03x and 0.88x; view 15.9 s (0.6.6) and 52.8 s (0.6.8-pre1) vs 77.8 s, 4.88x and 1.47x; markdup 197.1 s and 244.6 s vs 885.8 s for a four-stage samtools sort/fixmate/sort/markdup pipeline, 4.49x and 3.62x; sort 249.3 s and 327.2 s vs 146.7 s, so samtools 1.7 is 1.70x faster at 120 GB (all ratios derived from page data).
corrections.workload: sambamBench-nf (Nextflow) runs flagstat, index, markdup, name sort (-n/-N) and view to /dev/null on the ~4 GB ENCODE BAM ENCFF044SJL with 16 threads and 120 GB (cluster profile; workstation profile 8 CPUs/40 GB), one run per tool version; samtools-1.7 markdup is a name sort, fixmate -m, coordinate sort and markdup pipeline, while sambamba markdup reads the BAM directly.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: sambamba 0.6.6 and 0.6.8-pre1 and samtools 1.3 and 1.7 from grape/<tool>:<version> containers (build flags not published). sambamba's own release build uses ldc2 -O3 -release -enable-inlining -boundscheck=off (test/benchmark/stats.org); samtools 1.7's Makefile defaults to CFLAGS = -g -Wall -O2.
corrections.hardware: CRG cluster node, 16 CPUs and 120 GB RAM allocated to each task (CPU model not stated), per the sambamBench-nf README and nextflow.config cluster profile; the README's quoted figures may come from the unopened 'ws' (workstation, 8 CPUs, 40 GB) report.
corrections.caveats: The markdup baseline is crippled: the samtools-1.7 template does two full sorts plus fixmate before markdup, and its sort and fixmate steps pass '-@{task.cpus}' without the '$', so the thread count is never interpolated; the trace shows 102% CPU for that task versus 658-890% for sambamba. The README's sort claim (up to 2x faster at 120GB+) is contradicted by the 120 GB report, where samtools 1.7 sorts 1.70x faster. The view 4x win holds for sambamba 0.6.6 only (0.6.8-pre1 is 1.47x), and flagstat 1.4x holds for 0.6.8-pre1 only. One run per task, 2018 tool versions (samtools 1.7, sambamba 0.6.x), and the README's linked CRG report does not resolve (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND public-docs.crg.es). samtools is built at its -O2 default against sambamba's -O3 release build. The README says samtools 1.4 reached parity in many areas and that sambamba's original advantage was parallel BAM I/O; the gains are parallelism and pipeline differences, not D against C. htslib (samtools' library) is listed in wave 8.
corrections.why_faster: Parallel BAM decoding and encoding and multi-threaded record formatting in sambamba (sambamba view uses -t 16 while samtools 1.7 view reaches 193% CPU at -@16), plus an unequal markdup comparison (single-threaded samtools sort/fixmate/sort/markdup pipeline against sambamba's direct Picard-style markdup); not a D language effect.

notes: README numbers are first-party quotes of a CRG report that no longer resolves; the pipeline's accessible 16-CPU report shows real flagstat (1.49x) and view (1.47-4.88x) wins, parity on index, a samtools win on sort (1.70x), and a markdup win against a crippled single-threaded four-stage samtools pipeline. Downgraded for the overstated markdup and sort claims; tier B kept on the independent pipeline. Record shortcomings: crippled markdup baseline, contradicted sort claim, 2018 versions, single runs, samtools -O2 default against sambamba -O3, parallelism rather than a D language effect.

tier_reason: First-party numbers from the repo's own bench/bench_bzip2.zig with Zig 0.15.2 ReleaseFast and an Apple M4 Max stated, but the system bzip2 1.0.8 build flags are not stated and the harness is asymmetric (in-process Zig calls against a spawned bzip2 subprocess with file I/O), so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, mixed pattern, 3 iterations, 1 MB: single thread compress 18.64 vs 10.43 MB/s (1.79x), decompress 67.14 vs 69.38 MB/s (0.97x); threads=auto (16) compress 27.18 vs 10.33 MB/s (2.63x), decompress 0.99x. Across the README's 1-128 MB rows, single-thread compression is 1.72-1.79x faster but decompression is 0.76-0.82x of system bzip2 at 8 MB and above; with 16 threads compression reaches 15.10x at 128 MB (162.74 vs 10.77 MB/s) against single-threaded bzip2, against 115.61 MB/s for pbzip2 (1.41x over pbzip2, derived from page data), and pbzip2 decompresses up to 9.58x faster than bzip2 while bzip2z does not parallelise default single-stream decompression.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: bzip2z: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; system bzip2 1.0.8 and pbzip2 1.1.13 from a Nix dev shell (build flags not stated; bzip2 1.0.8's own Makefile defaults to -O2).
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 Max, Darwin 25.3.0 arm64, threads=auto resolved to 16, run 2026-01-15
corrections.caveats: Harness asymmetry: bench/bench_bzip2.zig times bzip2z as in-memory library calls but times system bzip2 and pbzip2 as subprocesses (process spawn, reading the temp input file and writing the .bz2 or output file), which favours bzip2z; even so its decompression is parity at 1 MB and 18-24% slower at 8-128 MB. The 'mixed' input is synthetic and 75% periodic (a-z cycle, XYXY, byte ramp, then random), a pattern that is bzip2's block-sort worst case and favours linear-time SA-IS. Three iterations of one pattern. Outputs are valid bzip2 but not byte-identical (sizes differ by under 0.2%); only bzip2z's round trip is checked. The threads rows add parallel block compression that stock bzip2 lacks; pbzip2 is the fair parallel comparison (bzip2z 1.41x at 128 MB compress, much slower to decompress). Numbers were recorded 2026-01-15 on Zig 0.15.2, while the current bench source uses the Zig 0.16 std.Io API and the code has changed since (70 commits, last 2026-10-10), so the table predates the current code. bzip2 likely built at -O2 against ReleaseFast. First-party, 1 star.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithmic: SA-IS linear-time suffix array construction for the BWT replaces bzip2's block sort (whose fallback path is slow on the periodic 'mixed' input), plus optional concurrent block compression; decompression, which shares bzip2's algorithm, is not faster.

notes: README numbers match the record's 1 MB rows; the larger rows show decompression 18-24% slower than C bzip2 and the 16-thread compression gain measured against single-threaded bzip2. Keep at C; shortcomings: subprocess against in-process timing, synthetic periodic input that is bzip2's worst case, algorithmic (SA-IS) rather than language win, slower decompression, numbers predate the current code, unknown bzip2 build flags.
